document_check.note: The document is Perez-Blanco, Felpete, Patten, Mallo, Pereiro, Campos-Magdaleno and Juncos-Rabadan, 'Do informant-reported subjective cognitive complaints predict progression to mild cognitive impairment and dementia better than self-reported complaints in old adults? A meta-analytical study', Ageing Research Reviews 82 (2022) 101772. The cited caveat about overlapping confidence intervals appears verbatim in the Conclusions (page 8).

cited_result: The comparison of pooled relative risks of progression from cognitively unimpaired to MCI and/or dementia: informant-reported SCCs RR 1.38 (95% CI 1.16 to 1.64) against self-reported SCCs RR 1.27 (95% CI 1.06 to 1.534). The authors conclude that the overlapping CIs preclude a decisive conclusion that informant report is more predictive.
tool_reason: The cited result is a random-effects meta-analysis within a systematic review, so ROBIS applies.

domains.rationale: The review was registered on PROSPERO and has detailed PICOTD-based criteria. However, the criteria as applied conflict with those written: studies with MCI at baseline and studies with only neuropsychological outcomes were included despite exclusion 5b and inclusion 4. The search was restricted to published articles. The effect on the cited CU-transition meta-analysis is probably limited.

signalling.question: 1.1 Did the review adhere to pre-defined objectives and eligibility criteria?
signalling.quote: The systematic review was conducted according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-analyses statement (PRISMA 2020) (Page et al., 2021) and registered in the international prospective register of systematic reviews (PROSPERO, with registration number CRD42021227459)

signalling.question: 1.2 Were the eligibility criteria appropriate for the review question?
signalling.quote: (2) prospective longitudinal studies including at least six months of follow-up; (3) studies including SCCs (identified by questions or questionnaires) reported by participants and informants; (4) studies reporting stability or progression of participants with SCCs to MCI and/ or dementia

signalling.question: 1.3 Were eligibility criteria unambiguous?
signalling.quote: (b) diagnosis of neurological disorder instilled or in the prodromal phase, including MCI ... [versus] five studies included CU individuals with SCCs and individuals diagnosed with MCI at baseline.

signalling.question: 1.4 Were all restrictions in eligibility criteria based on study characteristics appropriate?
signalling.quote: prospective longitudinal studies including at least six months of follow-up

signalling.question: 1.5 Were any restrictions in eligibility criteria based on sources of information appropriate?
signalling.quote: We searched published articles between 1987 (the earliest found) and November 2020

domains.rationale: Four relevant databases were searched with a structured Boolean strategy over a long date range, and screening was done in duplicate with a third reviewer. No supplementary search methods are reported, and the flow arithmetic contains small inconsistencies.

signalling.question: 2.1 Did the search include an appropriate range of databases/electronic sources for published and unpublished reports?
signalling.quote: they were selected from PsycINFO, PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science (WOS) databases of medical journals

signalling.question: 2.2 Were methods additional to database searching used to identify relevant reports?
signalling.quote: Searched for reference-list checking, citation tracking, contact with authors and grey literature. None reported.

signalling.question: 2.3 Were the terms and structure of the search strategy likely to retrieve as many eligible studies as possible?
signalling.quote: ("subjective decline" OR concern* OR complaint* OR SCD OR SMC OR SMD OR SCC) AND (risk OR association OR evolution OR progression OR conversion) AND (memory OR cogniti*) AND (dementia OR Alzheimer* OR MCI OR "mild cognitive impairment" OR "minor neurocognitive disorder" OR "major neurocognitive disorder") AND (informant* OR relative* OR partner OR "study partner")

signalling.question: 2.4 Were restrictions based on date, publication format, or language appropriate?
signalling.quote: We searched published articles between 1987 (the earliest found) and November 2020

signalling.question: 2.5 Were efforts made to minimise error in selection of studies?
signalling.quote: Two different researchers (L.P.-B. and A.F.) screened titles, abstracts and full-text articles. ... When any inconsistencies appeared, a final consensus was reached through discussion with a third reviewer (O.J.-R.)

domains.rationale: One reviewer extracted the data, with later discussion, and Table 1 contains internal inconsistencies. For two OR studies, CIs were back-calculated from p-values, no author contact for missing estimates is reported, and it is not stated whether adjusted or unadjusted estimates were taken. Study quality was assessed with an established tool and disagreements were reconciled.

signalling.question: 3.1 Were efforts made to minimise error in data collection?
signalling.quote: One reviewer (L. P.-B.) abstracted data from each study included. The data extracted were discussed with the third reviewer (O.J.-R.) and with a fourth researcher (S.C.M.).

signalling.question: 3.2 Were sufficient study characteristics available for both review authors and readers to be able to interpret the results?
signalling.quote: The characteristics of the studies included are summarised in Table 1.

signalling.question: 3.3 Were all relevant study results collected for use in the synthesis?
signalling.quote: The main reasons for excluding articles from the meta-analyses were no quantitative information was provided for either type of report, and no size measures (i.e., OR, HR) were provided.

signalling.question: 3.4 Was risk of bias (or methodological quality) formally assessed using appropriate criteria?
signalling.quote: Study quality was assessed using the quality assessment tool for observational cohort and cross-sectional studies from the National Heart, Lung and Blood Institute

signalling.question: 3.5 Were efforts made to minimise error in risk of bias assessment?
signalling.quote: The intersection point and classification of items 5 and 12 as "not applicable" were discussed, and disagreements were reconciled with the reviewers (O.J.-R. and S.C.M.).

domains.rationale: ORs and HRs were pooled as relative risks, and some CIs were imputed from p-values. Heterogeneity was high (I2 77.5% and 83.8%) and unexplored. There was no sensitivity analysis and no assessment of publication bias, and study quality was not used in the synthesis. The comparative question was answered by comparing two separately pooled estimates by eye, with no formal test of their difference.

signalling.question: 4.1 Did the synthesis include all studies that it should?
signalling.quote: Of these 14 studies, only 7 studies were included in the meta-analyses

signalling.question: 4.2 Were all pre-defined analyses reported or departures explained?
signalling.quote: Regarding adults with MCI, we were unable to carry out a meta-analysis because we only found four studies on this type of impairment

signalling.question: 4.3 Was the synthesis appropriate given the nature and similarity in the research questions, study designs and outcomes across included studies?
signalling.quote: The Odds Ratio (OR) or Hazard Ratio (HR) associated with the estimates were converted and interpreted as Relative Risk (RR), which was used as a measure of the effect size. ... Only one of the studies reporting OR provided confidence intervals and the other two studies only provided p- values. In order to include these studies, we estimated their 95% confidence intervals from the reported p-values.

signalling.question: 4.4 Was between-study variation (heterogeneity) minimal or addressed in the synthesis?
signalling.quote: In this analysis, the I2 value was 77.5% and tau2 value, 0.0318. ... In the analysis of informant report, the I2 value was 83.8%

signalling.question: 4.5 Were the findings robust, e.g. as demonstrated through funnel plot or sensitivity analyses?
signalling.quote: Another limitation of the study was that the number of studies was too small to enable use of funnel plots or other methods to detect publication bias.

signalling.question: 4.6 Were biases in primary studies minimal or addressed in the synthesis?
signalling.quote: Ten studies (71.42%) were qualified as of good quality, while three studies (21,42%) were valued as of poor quality.

domains.domain: Phase 3: risk of bias in the review
domains.rationale: The Conclusions properly hedge the comparison (this is the cited statement) and acknowledge the OR/HR mixing and the undetectable publication bias. But the Abstract and Discussion still call the informant association 'stronger and more robust', partly on the basis of p-values. The Discussion claims the data are unlikely to reflect sampling variability despite I2 above 75%, and neither heterogeneity nor study quality is carried into the interpretation.

signalling.question: A. Did the interpretation of findings address all of the concerns identified in Domains 1 to 4?
signalling.quote: Therefore, pooled estimates should be viewed with some caution. However, the association was consistently in the direction of increased risk, especially in the group with informant- reported cognitive decline, and the findings of the meta-analysis help to confirm that the reported data are unlikely to arise due to sampling variability.

signalling.question: B. Was the relevance of identified studies to the review's research question appropriately considered?
signalling.quote: Ten studies included a sample with CU older adults with SCCs who progressed to MCI and/or dementia ... The other five studies considered CU older adults with SCCs who underwent cognitive decline, taking into account the neuropsychological performance at follow-up

signalling.question: C. Did the reviewers avoid emphasising results on the basis of their statistical significance?
signalling.quote: thought surprisingly the association was stronger and more robust for informant- reported data [1.38, with a 95% CI of 1.16 –1.64, p < 0.001] than for self-reported data [1.27 (95% CI 1.06 – 1.534, p = 0.011].

applicability.rationale: The review's question (self- versus informant-reported SCCs predicting progression to MCI or dementia in cognitively unimpaired older adults) matches the use made of it. The outcome combines MCI and dementia transitions and includes community as well as clinical samples.

overall_rationale: The review was registered and used duplicate screening and a quality tool, but Domain 4 is high. ORs and HRs were pooled as RR with some CIs imputed from p-values, heterogeneity was high and unexplored, and there was no sensitivity or publication-bias analysis and no formal test of the self-versus-informant difference. Extraction by a single reviewer leaves Domain 3 unclear. The interpretation only partly addresses these concerns, although the specific caveat the review cites is the appropriate reading.
